extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of English literature; general educated readers interested in 18th-century drama and periodical essays
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and aesthetic guidance for writing and judging early-18th-century English comedies, adaptations, and periodical moral essays (as exemplified by Steele and Addison). Emphasises tone, moral seriousness, theatrical practicality, and audience considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive didacticism
rubrics_metrics.description: A didactic manner, marked by an 'air of superiority', is repugnant and weakens literary effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Steele's 'Christian Hero' was judged 'too didactic' — plain truth from the author's heart but showing an air of superiority. Anti-pattern: writing that reads like a professional teaching rules rather than engaging readers; such manner alienates rather than persuades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend humour with seriousness (earnest thought beneath gaiety)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy should rest on seriousness; gaiety and humour may be the surface, but there should be underlying earnest thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele's comedies are praised because 'each comedy of his was based on seriousness' — the gay manner does not conceal earnest thoughts. Benefit: gives wit moral weight and enduring value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid profanity and unwholesome expletives
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from oaths and vulgar expletives used merely for stage emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele's plays were 'wholly free from the garnish of oaths and unwholesome expletives which his contemporaries seemed to think essential to stage emphasis.' This restraint distinguished his work morally and aesthetically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mock sacred grief or trivialize serious subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the mockery and mummery of grief and the trivialization of matters that should be treated with seriousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In 'The Funeral' Steele censured mock grief; anti-pattern: treating sacred or solemn subjects as objects of mere raillery. Similarly, avoid mocking truth and justice by legal technicalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve comic genre — avoid turning comedy into morality play
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let earnest moralizing push a comedy beyond its bounds into 'excellent morality' that fails as art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Steele's alterations in 'The Lying Lover' made parts of the play 'beyond the bounds of comedy' — moral earnestness spoiled the comic art. Maintain genre conventions and comic structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt source material to contemporary moral/aesthetic expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: When adapting foreign or classical works, alter endings or emphases to suit the 'reforming age' and current moral tastes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele changed Corneille's close to accord with contemporary reforming sensibilities ('Pleasure must still have something that's severe'). Use adaptation to align source material with present ethical/aesthetic norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure theatrical clarity — make strokes visible to the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage writing must use sufficiently strong, broad strokes so that character and action register 'at a distance' to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addison observed plays were like a 'picture in which the strokes were not strong enough to appear at a distance.' Delicate touches risk being lost in performance; if writing is subtle, expect limited stage impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer natural, unforced humour; avoid contrived witticisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour should be 'easy and natural' rather than composed of 'studied similies and repartees' meant to pander to false taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addison praised the absence of 'studied similies and repartees' that indulge a false popular taste. Aim for effortless humour in the Molière vein rather than artificial cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider performance quality and audience sophistication
rubrics_metrics.description: Delicate humour and character touches require skilled actors and an audience able to discriminate; otherwise they may fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele/ Addision note that 'touches [are] too delicate for every taste in a popular assembly' and that good acting provides 'as just and good actions as ever I saw on the stage.' Tailor writing to likely performers and spectators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jarring stylistic or formal shifts that disrupt tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden changes in style or metre (e.g., inserting blank verse in a comic scene) can rupture comic tone and audience expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele's use of blank verse in the Newgate scene of 'The Lying Lover' changed the play's tone and contributed to its being 'damned for its piety.' Maintain stylistic consistency appropriate to genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use wit to serve moral or religious sentiment without cant
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit can and should support moral or religious aims, but avoid 'mere religious cant' or preachiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele's work is praised for giving 'a lively wit to the true service of religion, without having spoken or written ... a word of mere religious cant.' Effective moral writing is persuasive, not sanctimonious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray social institutions (e.g., marriage) with respect and counter frivolous ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: Literature should contend against frivolous and vicious ridicule of institutions like marriage and uphold their honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele 'made it a duty of his literary life to contend against the frivolous and vicious ridicule of the ties of marriage' — depict marital and domestic ties sympathetically rather than satirically for cheap effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patriotism can be a valuable theme but carries political risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Patriotic feeling in writing may attract approval and define character, but may also provoke party conflict and political consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele's patriotism (e.g., characterising King William) brought notice and popularity but also political entanglements; use patriotic themes knowingly and be prepared for partisan reaction.
